steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on polynomial-time algorithms for attributed graph alignment. Motivate the problem with social network de-anonymization, define the attributed Erdős–Rényi pair model, review what is known about information-theoretic limits and efficient algorithms, introduce our two algorithms and their feasible regions, and explain what attributes buy when computation is limited.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Graph alignment and attributed graph alignment: motivation
2. The attributed Erdős–Rényi pair model
3. Two central questions: information-theoretic vs. polynomial-time feasibility
4. Prior work without attributes and with attributes
5. Our algorithms AttrRich and AttrSparse
6. Feasible regions, gap, seeded alignment
7. Impact of attributes under computational constraints (Figure 2)

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation
- graph alignment = graph matching = noisy graph isomorphism: vertex correspondence between two correlated graphs
- growing attention: social network de-anonymization
- anonymized social network datasets; attacker aligns user-user graph with public data
- attributed graph alignment: attributes of vertices also public, besides user-user connections
- e.g. anonymized Netflix network: movie-watching history and ratings public
- model gives achievability + converse results for variants of Erdős–Rényi graph alignment: no attributes, seeded, bipartite -> integrated framework

2. Model \mathcal{G}(n,p,s_{\mathrm{u}};m,q,s_{\mathrm{a}}), first proposed in prior work
- base graph G on [n+m]; [n] users, rest attributes
- user-user edges i.i.d. with prob p; user-attribute edges i.i.d. with prob q; no attribute-attribute edges
- subsample to G_{1}, G_{2}: user-user with s_{\mathrm{u}}, user-attribute with s_{\mathrm{a}}
- uniform random permutation \Pi^{*} on users of G_{2} -> G_{2}^{\prime}
- goal: exact alignment, recover \Pi^{*} from G_{1} and G_{2}^{\prime}

3. Two questions
- feasible with unlimited computation? information-theoretically feasible region / information-theoretic limits
- feasible with polynomial-time algorithms? feasible region of polynomial-time algorithms
- characterizing both + relationship: fundamental understanding

4. Prior work
- without attributes, information-theoretic limits: exact alignment feasible when intersection graph dense enough; sharp threshold, some gap between converse and achievability
- polynomial-time algorithms: need higher edge correlation; open whether they reach the limits
- attributed: information-theoretic limit studied; feasible/infeasible regions with a gap in some regimes
- polynomial-time feasible region for attributed alignment not studied -> our focus

5. Our algorithms
- two polynomial-time algorithms, feasible regions characterized
- AttrRich: mqs_{\mathrm{a}}^{2}=\Omega(\log n), attribute-information rich regime
- AttrSparse: mqs_{\mathrm{a}}^{2}=o(\log n), attribute-information sparse regime
- step 1: user-attribute connections -> anchor users; step 2: user-user connections to anchors align the rest
- AttrRich gets much larger anchor set; uses one-hop connections; AttrSparse one-hop or multiple-hop depending on sparsity
- common neighbor witnesses idea from seeded graph alignment; here two-step procedure, careful treatment of dependency between steps

6. Feasible regions
- Figure 1: AttrRich = area 2, AttrSparse = area 3; information-theoretic regions from prior work for comparison
- gap to information-theoretically feasible region; open whether fundamental for polynomial-time algorithms
- specialization to seeded Erdős–Rényi alignment: includes range of parameters not known achievable before

7. Impact of attributes (Figure 2)
- attributes may help much more when computational efficiency is priority
- sparse regime np=\Theta(\log n)
- 2(a): mqs_{\mathrm{a}}^{2}=0, no attribute info; 2(b): mqs_{\mathrm{a}}^{2}=0.1\log n
- p=o(1); nps_{\mathrm{u}}/\log n arbitrarily large constant, not tending to infinity
- information-theoretic limits in n,p and s_{\mathrm{u}} improve a bit
- bigger improvement: polynomial-time feasible region
- 2(a): green region above s_{\mathrm{u}}=\sqrt{\alpha} achievable by known algorithm; \alpha\approx 0.338 Otter's constant; red region below not known achievable, conjectured infeasible
- 2(b): green region above information theoretic limit (dotted curve) achievable by AttrRich (q=o(1), s_{\mathrm{a}}=\Theta(1))
- if \sqrt{\alpha} is right threshold, small amount of attribute info lowers it to arbitrarily small constant

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The graph alignment problem, which is also called the graph matching or noisy graph isomorphism problem, is about finding the correspondence between the vertices of two correlated graphs. The problem has received more and more attention because of its applications in social network de-anonymization. For example, social network datasets are usually anonymized to protect privacy. But an attacker may be able to de-anonymize the dataset by aligning its user-user connection graph with the one of publicly available data. Attributed graph alignment is a variant of graph alignment where side information, called attributes of vertices, is also publicly available in addition to the user-user connection information. The motivation for this variant is that there might be publicly available attribute information in social networks. For example, in the anonymized Netflix network the users' movie-watching history and ratings are publicly available. Also, studying the proposed model gives both achievability and converse results for several well-known variations of the Erdős–Rényi graph alignment problems, namely the traditional graph alignment problem without attributes, the seeded graph alignment problem, and the bipartite alignment problem. So studying attributed graph alignment gives a new perspective for investigating these problems in one integrated framework.

In this paper we focus on the attributed graph alignment problem under the attributed Erdős–Rényi pair model \mathcal{G}(n,p,s_{\mathrm{u}};m,q,s_{\mathrm{a}}), which was first proposed in earlier work. In this model a base graph G is generated on the vertex set [n+m], where the vertices from the set [n] are users and the other vertices are attributes. Between each pair of users an edge is generated independently and identically with probability p, representing their connection. For each user-attribute pair an edge is generated independently and identically with probability q, representing their association. There are no edges between attributes. Then the graph G is independently subsampled to two graphs G_{1} and G_{2}, where each user-user edge is subsampled with probability s_{\mathrm{u}} and each user-attribute edge is subsampled with probability s_{\mathrm{a}}. To model the anonymization, a random permutation \Pi^{*} chosen uniformly at random is applied to the users in G_{2}, which generates an anonymized version G_{2}^{\prime}. Our goal is exact alignment, i.e., recovering the permutation \Pi^{*} exactly using G_{1} and G_{2}^{\prime}.

For attributed graph alignment, and for graph alignment in general, two questions are often asked. First, for what region of graph statistics is exact alignment feasible if we have unlimited computational power? This region is usually called the information-theoretically feasible region or the information-theoretic limits. Second, for what region of graph statistics is exact alignment feasible with polynomial-time algorithms? This is usually called the feasible region of polynomial-time algorithms. Characterizing these two feasible regions and how they relate is very important for a fundamental understanding of the graph alignment problem.

These two questions have been studied extensively under the Erdős–Rényi pair model without attributes. One line of research looks at the information-theoretic limits of exact alignment. Roughly, it is shown that exact alignment is information-theoretically feasible when the intersection graph is dense enough. A sharp threshold of exact alignment has been established, but there is still some gap between the converse and the achievability results. Another line of research looks at polynomial-time algorithms for exact alignment. The existing polynomial-time algorithms need higher edge correlation between the two graphs than the information-theoretic limits to achieve exact alignment. Whether there are polynomial-time algorithms that achieve the known information-theoretic limits is still an open question.

- AttrSparse: mqs_{\mathrm{a}}^{2}=o(\log n), attribute-information sparse regime

- AttrRich gets much larger anchor set; uses one-hop connections; AttrSparse one-hop or multiple-hop depending on sparsity
- common neighbor witnesses idea from seeded graph alignment; here two-step procedure, careful treatment of dependency between steps

6. Feasible regions
- Figure 1: AttrRich = area 2, AttrSparse = area 3; information-theoretic regions from prior work for comparison
- gap to information-theoretically feasible region; open whether fundamental for polynomial-time algorithms
- specialization to seeded Erdős–Rényi alignment: includes range of parameters not known achievable before

7. Impact of attributes (Figure 2)
- attributes may help much more when computational efficiency is priority
- sparse regime np=\Theta(\log n)

Our goal is exact alignment, i.e., recovering the permutation \Pi^{*} exactly using G_{1} and G_{2}^{\prime}.

For attributed graph alignment, and for graph alignment in general, two questions are often asked. First, for what region of graph statistics is exact alignment feasible if we have unlimited computational power? This region is usually called the information-theoretically feasible region or the information-theoretic limits. Second, for what region of graph statistics is exact alignment feasible with polynomial-time algorithms? This is usually called the feasible region of polynomial-time algorithms. Characterizing these two feasible regions and how they relate is very important for a fundamental understanding of the graph alignment problem.

These two questions have been studied extensively under the Erdős–Rényi pair model without attributes. One line of research looks at the information-theoretic limits of exact alignment. Roughly, it is shown that exact alignment is information-theoretically feasible when the intersection graph is dense enough. A sharp threshold of exact alignment has been established, but there is still some gap between the converse and the achievability results. Another line of research looks at polynomial-time algorithms for exact alignment. The existing polynomial-time algorithms need higher edge correlation between the two graphs than the information-theoretic limits to achieve exact alignment. Whether there are polynomial-time algorithms that achieve the known information-theoretic limits is still an open question.

For attributed graph alignment, the information-theoretic limit has been studied in earlier work, where the feasible region (achievability results) and the infeasible region (converse results) are characterized, with a gap between them in some regimes. But the feasible region of polynomial-time algorithms for attributed graph alignment has not been studied before, and this is what this paper focuses on. We propose two polynomial-time algorithms for attributed graph alignment and characterize their feasible regions. The two algorithms are designed for two different regimes of parameters, depending on how rich the attribute information is. The algorithm AttrRich is for the regime where mqs_{\mathrm{a}}^{2}=\Omega(\log n), which we call the attribute-information rich regime, and the algorithm AttrSparse is for the regime where mqs_{\mathrm{a}}^{2}=o(\log n), which we call the attribute-information sparse regime. Both algorithms first use the user-attribute connections to align a set of anchor users, and then use the user-user connections to the anchors to align the rest of the users. Because the regimes are different, AttrRich can generate a much larger set of anchors in the first step than AttrSparse. So AttrRich and AttrSparse use the anchors differently in the second step: AttrRich uses one-hop user-user connections to align the rest of the users, while AttrSparse uses one-hop or multiple-hop user-user connections depending on how sparse the user-user connections are. The idea of matching vertices based on common neighbor witnesses has been used to construct efficient graph alignment algorithms in the context of seeded graph alignment. Here we use this idea in a two-step procedure in the setting of attributed graphs, and we analyze its performance by carefully treating the dependency between the two steps.

Figure 1 shows our characterizations of the feasible regions of AttrRich and AttrSparse as areas 2 and 3. For comparison the figure also shows the information-theoretically feasible and infeasible regions given in earlier work. There is a gap between the feasible region achieved by AttrRich and AttrSparse and the known information-theoretically feasible region. Whether this gap is a fundamental limit of polynomial-time algorithms is left open.

We also specialize the feasible region of the proposed algorithms to the seeded Erdős–Rényi graph alignment problem, and show that the specialized feasible region includes a certain range of parameters that is not known to be achievable in the literature.

Our results show that attributes may help graph alignment in a much more significant way when computational efficiency is a priority. Figure 2 shows this possible impact of attributes in the sparse regime np=\Theta(\log n). In Figure 2(a) we let mqs_{\mathrm{a}}^{2}=0, so the attributes give no information, which is the same as the graph alignment problem without attributes. In Figure 2(b) we let mqs_{\mathrm{a}}^{2}=0.1\log n. To make the comparison easier, in both settings we keep p=o(1) and assume that the value of nps_{\mathrm{u}}/\log n can be an arbitrarily large constant but does not tend to infinity. Comparing the two figures, when mqs_{\mathrm{a}}^{2} increases from 0 to 0.1\log n, the information-theoretic limits in terms of the user-user parameters (n,p and s_{\mathrm{u}}) improve a bit, as expected. But the more fundamental improvement is in the feasible region of polynomial-time algorithms. In Figure 2(a), the green region above s_{\mathrm{u}}=\sqrt{\alpha} is achievable by a polynomial-time algorithm proposed in another work, where \alpha\approx 0.338 is known as Otter's constant. The red region below s_{\mathrm{u}}=\sqrt{\alpha} is not known to be achievable by any polynomial-time algorithm. In fact, this red region has been conjectured elsewhere to be infeasible for any polynomial-time algorithm. In Figure 2(b), on the other hand, the green region above the information theoretic limit, shown as the dotted curve, is achievable by our polynomial-time algorithm AttrRich (assuming q=o(1) and s_{\mathrm{a}}=\Theta(1)). So if \sqrt{\alpha} really is the right threshold between achievable and impossible for polynomial-time algorithms for graph alignment without attributes in the sparse regime, then a small amount of attribute information lowers this threshold to an arbitrarily small constant.

steps.text:
The graph alignment problem, also referred to as the graph matching or noisy graph isomorphism problem, is the problem of finding the correspondence between the vertices of two correlated graphs. This problem has been given increasing attention for its applications in social network de-anonymization. For instance, datasets of social networks are typically anonymized for privacy protection. However, an attacker may be able to de-anonymize the dataset by aligning its user-user connection graph with that of publicly available data. Attributed graph alignment is a variant of graph alignment in which side information, referred to as attributes of vertices, is also publicly available in addition to the user-user connection information. This variant is motivated by the fact that publicly available attribute information might exist in social networks. For example, the anonymized network Netflix has users' movie-watching history and ratings publicly available. Moreover, the examination of the proposed model provides both achievability and converse results for various well-known variations of the Erdős–Rényi graph alignment problems, including the traditional graph alignment problem without attributes, the seeded graph alignment problem, and the bipartite alignment problem. Consequently, the study of attributed graph alignment introduces a new perspective for investigating these problems within an integrated framework.

In this paper, we focus on the attributed graph alignment problem under the attributed Erdős–Rényi pair model \mathcal{G}(n,p,s_{\mathrm{u}};m,q,s_{\mathrm{a}}), first proposed in [1]. In this model, a base graph G is generated on the vertex set [n+m], where the vertices from the set [n] represent users and the rest of the vertices represent attributes. Between each pair of users, an edge is generated independently and identically with probability p to represent their connection. For each user-attribute pair, an edge is generated independently and identically with probability q to represent their association. Note that there are no edges between attributes. The graph G is then independently subsampled to two graphs G_{1} and G_{2}, where each user-user edge is subsampled with probability s_{\mathrm{u}} and each user-attribute edge is subsampled with probability s_{\mathrm{a}}. To model the anonymization procedure, a random permutation \Pi^{*} chosen uniformly at random is applied to the users in G_{2} to generate an anonymized version G_{2}^{\prime}. Our goal is to achieve exact alignment, i.e., to exactly recover the permutation \Pi^{*} using G_{1} and G_{2}^{\prime}.

For the attributed graph alignment problem, and for the graph alignment problem in general, two questions are often asked. First, for what region of graph statistics is exact alignment feasible with unlimited computational power? This region is usually referred to as the information-theoretically feasible region or the information-theoretic limits. Second, for what region of graph statistics is exact alignment feasible with polynomial-time algorithms? This region is usually referred to as the feasible region of polynomial-time algorithms. Characterizing these two feasible regions and their relationship is of great importance to a fundamental understanding of the graph alignment problem.

There have been extensive studies on these two questions under the Erdős–Rényi pair model without attributes. One line of research focuses on the information-theoretic limits of exact alignment [2,3,4,5]. Roughly speaking, it is shown that exact alignment is information-theoretically feasible when the intersection graph is dense enough. A sharp threshold of exact alignment has been established, while some gap still exists between the converse and the achievability results. Another line of research focuses on polynomial-time algorithms for exact alignment [6,7,8,9,10]. Compared to the information-theoretic limits, the existing polynomial-time algorithms require higher edge correlation between the pair of graphs to achieve exact alignment. Whether there exist polynomial-time algorithms that achieve the known information-theoretic limits is still an open question.

For the attributed graph alignment problem, the information-theoretic limit has been studied in [1], where the feasible region (achievability results) and the infeasible region (converse results) are characterized with a gap in between in some regimes. However, the feasible region of polynomial-time algorithms for attributed graph alignment has not been studied before, and it is the focus of this paper. In this work, we propose two polynomial-time algorithms for attributed graph alignment and characterize their feasible regions. The two algorithms are designed for two different regimes of parameters based on the richness of attribute information: the algorithm AttrRich is designed for the regime where mqs_{\mathrm{a}}^{2}=\Omega(\log n), referred to as the attribute-information rich regime, and the algorithm AttrSparse is designed for the regime where mqs_{\mathrm{a}}^{2}=o(\log n), referred to as the attribute-information sparse regime. In both algorithms, we first use the user-attribute connections to align a set of anchor users, and then use the user-user connections to the anchors to align the rest of the users. Due to the regime difference, AttrRich is able to generate a much larger set of anchors in the first step than AttrSparse. Therefore, the two algorithms use the anchors differently in the second step: AttrRich explores one-hop user-user connections to align the rest of the users, while AttrSparse explores one-hop or multiple-hop user-user connections depending on the sparsity of user-user connections. This idea of matching vertices based on common neighbor witnesses has been explored to construct efficient graph alignment algorithms in the context of seeded graph alignment [11,12,13,14]. In this work, we employ this idea in a two-step procedure in the setting of attributed graphs, and analyze its performance through a careful treatment of the dependency between the two steps.

Our characterizations of the feasible regions of AttrRich and AttrSparse are illustrated in Figure 1 as areas 2 and 3, respectively. The information-theoretically feasible and infeasible regions given in [1] are also shown in the figure for comparison. There is a gap between the feasible region achieved by AttrRich and AttrSparse and the known information-theoretically feasible region. It is left open whether this gap is a fundamental limit of polynomial-time algorithms.

In addition, we specialize the feasible region of the proposed algorithms to the seeded Erdős–Rényi graph alignment problem, and show that the specialized feasible region includes a certain range of parameters that is not known to be achievable in the literature.

Our results reveal that attributes may facilitate graph alignment in a much more significant way when computational efficiency is a priority. We demonstrate this possible impact of attributes under the sparse regime np=\Theta(\log n) in Figure 2. In Figure 2(a), we let mqs_{\mathrm{a}}^{2}=0, so there is no information from the attributes, which is equivalent to the graph alignment problem without attributes; in Figure 2(b), we let mqs_{\mathrm{a}}^{2}=0.1\log n. For ease of comparison, in both settings we keep p=o(1) and assume that the value of nps_{\mathrm{u}}/\log n can be an arbitrarily large constant but does not tend to infinity. Comparing the two figures, when mqs_{\mathrm{a}}^{2} increases from 0 to 0.1\log n, the information-theoretic limits in terms of the user-user parameters (n,p and s_{\mathrm{u}}) improve a bit, as expected. However, a more fundamental improvement is in the feasible region achievable by polynomial-time algorithms. In Figure 2(a), the green region above s_{\mathrm{u}}=\sqrt{\alpha} is achievable by a polynomial-time algorithm proposed in [10], where \alpha\approx 0.338 is known as Otter's constant. The red region below s_{\mathrm{u}}=\sqrt{\alpha} is not known to be achievable by any polynomial-time algorithm, and in [18] it is conjectured to be infeasible for any polynomial-time algorithm. In comparison, in Figure 2(b), the green region above the information theoretic limit, shown as the dotted curve, is achievable by our proposed polynomial-time algorithm AttrRich (assuming q=o(1) and s_{\mathrm{a}}=\Theta(1)). Therefore, if \sqrt{\alpha} is indeed the right threshold between achievable and impossible for polynomial-time algorithms for graph alignment without attributes in the sparse regime, a small amount of attribute information lowers this threshold to an arbitrarily small constant.
